title: Rylands v Fletcher
subtitle: Strict liability for escapes, and its quiet absorption into nuisance
objectives: State the elements of the rule in Rylands v Fletcher in full, including the foreseeability of damage requirement added by Cambridge Water
Explain why Transco v Stockport MBC narrowed 'non-natural use' and recharacterised the rule as a sub-species of nuisance rather than a freestanding strict liability tort
Identify what must actually 'escape' for the rule to apply, using Stannard v Gore's treatment of fire

leadingAuthorities.role: Origin of the rule: liability for the escape of a dangerous thing accumulated on land

leadingAuthorities.citation: Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather plc [1994] 2 AC 264
leadingAuthorities.role: Adds a requirement that the type of damage caused by the escape be reasonably foreseeable

leadingAuthorities.citation: Transco plc v Stockport MBC [2003] UKHL 61
leadingAuthorities.role: Narrows 'non-natural use' and recasts the rule as an extension of nuisance, not a distinct strict liability tort

leadingAuthorities.citation: Stannard (t/a Wyvern Tyres) v Gore [2012] EWCA Civ 1248
leadingAuthorities.role: Clarifies what must 'escape': the dangerous thing itself, not fire that happens to start in it

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Rylands v Fletcher looks, on the surface, like a strict liability tort with a fixed checklist — which is exactly how students lose marks on it. Since Transco, the real skill is knowing how narrowly 'non-natural use' now bites, and that the whole tort is best understood as a specialised branch of nuisance.

profileHooks.weakApplication: The elements themselves are stable, but 'non-natural use' post-Transco is judged far more narrowly than the 1868 case suggests. Watch how the worked examples treat ordinary domestic and commercial uses as natural, almost by default.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and get the 1868 facts fixed clearly in mind before Part 2 restates them as elements — the doctrine only makes sense once you can picture Fletcher's flooded mine.

overview.hook: In 1860s Lancashire, a mill owner built a reservoir to power his machinery. His contractors, digging the foundations, found old mine shafts beneath the site and — carelessly, but not maliciously — failed to seal them properly. When the reservoir filled, water poured down the shafts and flooded a neighbouring coal mine. No one had trespassed. No one had been negligent in any way the law could easily pin down. And yet a new rule of liability was born from that flood, one still cited in judgments today — even as, quietly, the courts have spent the last two decades narrowing it almost back out of existence.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 22 September 2026. The rule in Rylands v Fletcher remains good law but is now understood, following Transco v Stockport MBC, as a narrow sub-species of nuisance rather than a freestanding tort.

parts.heading: The flood at Fletcher's mine
parts.voice: historical-narrative — tells the origin story in sequence, like a case report
body: John Rylands owned a mill and, to power it, commissioned a reservoir on his land. The independent contractors he engaged to build it discovered, during construction, a series of disused mine shafts running beneath the reservoir site — shafts that connected, underground, to a working coal mine owned by Thomas Fletcher next door. The contractors did not seal the shafts properly. When the reservoir was filled with water, it burst through the old shafts and flooded Fletcher's mine.

Rylands himself had done nothing careless — he had engaged competent contractors and had no personal knowledge of the shafts. This was precisely the difficulty: ordinary negligence, which requires proof of a want of reasonable care by the defendant personally or someone for whom he was vicariously liable in a way the law then recognised, did not comfortably fit facts where the immediate fault, if any, lay with independent contractors. Trespass didn't fit either, since the flood was not a direct application of force but the consequence of water escaping.

Blackburn J, giving the judgment of the Court of Exchequer Chamber, reached for a different, broader principle: a person who, for their own purposes, brings onto their land and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at their peril, and is answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape. The House of Lords affirmed this on appeal, with Lord Cairns adding an important qualification that would later dominate the doctrine's development: the rule applies only where the defendant's use of the land was a 'non-natural' one.

components.term: The rule in Rylands v Fletcher
components.definition: A person who brings onto their land and keeps there something likely to do mischief if it escapes is strictly liable for damage caused by its escape, provided the use of the land was non-natural.

components.court: House of Lords (affirming the Court of Exchequer Chamber)
components.factsShort: A reservoir built to power a mill burst through disused mine shafts and flooded a neighbouring coal mine.
components.ratioShort: A defendant who brings and keeps on their land something likely to cause mischief if it escapes is strictly liable for its escape, where the use of the land is non-natural.

expanded.facts: Rylands's independent contractors built a reservoir on his land, unaware that disused mine shafts beneath the site connected to Fletcher's working mine next door. The shafts were not properly sealed, and when the reservoir filled, water burst through and flooded Fletcher's mine.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Blackburn J formulated the principle that a person who brings onto their land, for their own purposes, something likely to do mischief if it escapes, keeps it at their peril, and is liable for all the natural consequences of its escape. On appeal, Lord Cairns agreed but added that the rule applies only where the defendant's use of the land is a 'non-natural' one, distinguishing it from an ordinary use.
expanded.significance: This is the foundational statement of the rule, but read it knowing it will be substantially reshaped by Cambridge Water and Transco later in this lesson — the 1868 formulation is the starting point of the doctrine's history, not its current, settled shape.

interaction.prompt: Put the events of Rylands v Fletcher in the order they happened.
items: Contractors build a reservoir on Rylands's land
Old mine shafts beneath the site are found but not properly sealed
The reservoir is filled with water
Water bursts through the shafts and floods Fletcher's mine
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence — and notice the fault, if any, sits with the contractors' failure to seal the shafts, not with any deliberate act by Rylands, which is exactly why the courts needed a new principle rather than relying on ordinary negligence or trespass.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the shafts are discovered during construction, before the reservoir is filled; the flood only happens once the reservoir holds water and finds its way through the unsealed shafts.

parts.heading: The rule, broken into elements
parts.voice: structural — a checklist part for revision
body: Strip the story away and the rule in Rylands v Fletcher, as it stands today, has four elements a claimant must establish. Treat this as the skeleton the rest of the lesson puts flesh on.

First, the defendant must have brought onto their land, and kept there, something likely to do mischief if it escapes — this can be almost anything capable of causing harm once loose, historically water, but extending to gas, electricity, chemicals, and more. Second, the use of the land on which the thing is kept must be non-natural — a term explored in detail in Part 4, and narrowed considerably since 1868. Third, the thing must actually escape from land the defendant controls to land or property outside that control — an internal event, contained entirely within the defendant's own land, does not engage the rule at all. Fourth, following Cambridge Water, the damage caused must be of a type that was reasonably foreseeable as a consequence of the escape, even though the tort is otherwise strict as to fault.

components.label: Elements of the rule in Rylands v Fletcher
points: The defendant brings onto their land, and keeps there, something likely to do mischief if it escapes
The use of the land is non-natural
The thing escapes from land under the defendant's control to land or property outside it
The damage caused is of a type that was reasonably foreseeable as a result of the escape (Cambridge Water)

interaction.prompt: A chemical is stored safely inside a factory and spills onto the factory's own floor, causing no damage beyond the building. Has there been an 'escape' for Rylands v Fletcher purposes?
options: No — the chemical never left land under the defendant's control
Yes — any spillage of a dangerous substance is automatically an escape
It depends only on whether the chemical was dangerous
interaction.trapExplanation: Students often treat any spillage or release as an 'escape'. The rule requires the thing to move from land the defendant controls to land or property outside that control — a spill fully contained within the defendant's own premises, however dangerous the substance, does not satisfy this element.

parts.heading: When the damage wasn't foreseeable at all
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through a slow-moving environmental case
body: Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather looks, on its facts, nothing like a burst reservoir — which is exactly why it matters. A tanning business used a solvent, perchloroethylene, in its manufacturing process over many years. Small quantities spilled repeatedly onto the factory floor during ordinary use and, over time, seeped down through the ground, eventually contaminating a borehole used by a water company more than a mile away, forcing it to find an alternative source at considerable expense.

At the time the spillages occurred, nobody — including with the best available scientific and technical knowledge — could have foreseen that solvent spilled onto a concrete floor would migrate that far through the ground and contaminate a distant water supply in that way. The water company nonetheless argued that Rylands v Fletcher was a strict liability rule: once an escape and resulting damage were shown, foreseeability of the type of harm shouldn't matter at all.

The House of Lords disagreed, and in doing so reshaped the tort. Lord Goff held that liability under Rylands v Fletcher should be aligned with the ordinary law of nuisance, from which the rule had, historically, developed — and nuisance itself requires that the type of damage be reasonably foreseeable, even where fault as to how the damage occurred is not required. Because the contamination of a distant water supply by gradual seepage was not, on the facts as they stood at the relevant time, a foreseeable type of damage, the claim failed. The case matters for its result, but matters more for what it reveals: Rylands v Fletcher was never quite the pure strict liability outlier it is sometimes taught as — it was always closer to nuisance than to something like liability for keeping a dangerous animal.

components.caseName: Cambridge Water Co v Eastern Counties Leather plc
components.factsShort: Solvent spilled during a tannery's manufacturing process seeped through the ground over years and contaminated a distant water company's borehole.
components.ratioShort: Liability under Rylands v Fletcher requires that the type of damage caused by the escape be reasonably foreseeable — the rule is not strict as to the kind of harm, only as to fault in causing it.

expanded.facts: Small, repeated spillages of a solvent used in leather tanning seeped through the factory floor and migrated through the ground over a long period, eventually reaching and contaminating a borehole used by a water company more than a mile away.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Goff held that Rylands v Fletcher liability should develop in line with nuisance, requiring the type of damage to be reasonably foreseeable at the time of the relevant conduct, even though the tort remains strict as to whether the defendant was at fault in causing the escape itself. Because the manner and extent of the contamination were not foreseeable on the scientific knowledge available at the time, the claim failed.
expanded.significance: This is the case that inserted a foreseeability filter into what had looked like a pure strict liability rule, and it is the first major step towards Transco's later conclusion that Rylands v Fletcher is best understood as a specialised extension of nuisance rather than a standalone tort.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that ultimately defeats the claim in Cambridge Water.
interaction.scenarioText: The tannery used a solvent as part of its ordinary manufacturing process. Small amounts spilled onto the factory floor repeatedly over the years. The solvent seeped through the ground and eventually contaminated a borehole over a mile away. At the time the spillages occurred, this type of long-distance contamination could not reasonably have been foreseen.
tappableSpans: spilled onto the factory floor repeatedly
contaminated a borehole over a mile away
could not reasonably have been foreseen
interaction.correctSpan: could not reasonably have been foreseen
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The claim doesn't fail for lack of an escape or lack of damage — both are present. It fails because the type of damage was not reasonably foreseeable at the relevant time, which Cambridge Water made an essential element of the tort.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what actually defeats the claim. The escape happened, and the damage was real — what's missing is foreseeability of that type of damage at the time of the spillages, which Cambridge Water requires.

parts.heading: What counts as 'non-natural' now?
parts.voice: analytical — builds the modern test step by step, comparing old and new understanding
body: Transco v Stockport MBC is the case that did the most damage to the idea that Rylands v Fletcher is a broad, general-purpose strict liability tort. A water pipe supplying a block of flats developed a leak. The leaking water saturated an embankment, which then collapsed, exposing a gas pipe belonging to Transco and requiring it to carry out urgent remedial works. Transco sued the local authority in Rylands v Fletcher, arguing that laying and maintaining a water pipe to serve the flats was an accumulation of something likely to cause mischief if it escaped.

The House of Lords rejected the claim, and in doing so restated the whole doctrine narrowly. Lord Bingham held that ordinary domestic water supply — the kind of thing found in essentially every residential building — could not sensibly be treated as a 'non-natural' use of land, however much mischief the water caused once it escaped. Non-natural use, on the modern test, requires something extraordinary or unusual, judged by reference to the time and place in question, that creates an increased risk to others; it is not enough that the thing is man-made, or that its escape happened to cause serious damage.

The more structurally important move in Transco is Lord Bingham's characterisation of the tort itself: he described Rylands v Fletcher as best understood as a sub-species of nuisance, applying nuisance-like principles to isolated escapes rather than continuing states of affairs, rather than as a freestanding strict liability tort with its own independent life. That framing matters for how the whole doctrine should be approached — not as an exception to fault-based liability sitting apart from the rest of tort, but as nuisance's answer to the single, isolated event.

components.title: Assessing 'non-natural use' after Transco
components.description: A decision path for whether a use of land is non-natural for Rylands v Fletcher purposes.

nodes.label: Is the use of the land an ordinary one for its time and place (e.g. domestic water supply, ordinary storage)?
Yes → natural use; Rylands v Fletcher does not apply, whatever mischief resulted
No → does the use create an increased risk to others beyond what is ordinary for the locality?
Yes → capable of being a non-natural use

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the use of the land is ordinary for its time and place, such as domestic water supply or ordinary storage — if so, it is a natural use and Rylands v Fletcher does not apply, regardless of the mischief that resulted. If the use is not ordinary, ask whether it creates an increased risk to others beyond what is normal for the locality; only then is it capable of being treated as a non-natural use.

components.label: Transco's two contributions
points: Narrows 'non-natural use' to something extraordinary or unusual for the time and place, creating an increased risk — ordinary domestic and commercial uses do not qualify merely because something went wrong
Reclassifies Rylands v Fletcher as a sub-species of nuisance dealing with isolated escapes, not a freestanding strict liability tort

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that, after Transco, an ordinary domestic water supply pipe serving a block of flats counts as a 'non-natural use' of land?
interaction.explanation: Transco held that laying and maintaining an ordinary domestic water supply is a natural use of land, however serious the consequences when it fails — non-natural use requires something extraordinary for the time and place, not simply something that happens to escape and cause damage.

parts.heading: Fire, tyres, and what actually has to escape
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap examiners return to
body: One more case earns its place here because it exposes a distinction students routinely miss: it is not enough that something dangerous is on the defendant's land and a fire later spreads from it. The thing the defendant accumulated must itself be what escapes.

In Stannard v Gore, the defendant ran a tyre-fitting business and stored a very large quantity of tyres on his premises. A fire started accidentally — not through any non-natural use directly causing the ignition — and spread rapidly through the stored tyres, then onto neighbouring property. The claimant argued Rylands v Fletcher applied: tyres in that quantity were something likely to do mischief if they caught fire, kept on the land for the defendant's purposes.

The Court of Appeal rejected the claim. The 'thing' the defendant had brought onto and kept on his land was the tyres — and the tyres themselves never escaped; they burned in place. What escaped was the fire, and fire is not itself a thing the defendant 'accumulated' in the relevant sense unless the defendant brought something onto the land that was itself dangerously likely to ignite and spread, such as a large stock of a highly flammable chemical. Storing an ordinary quantity of tyres, however large, was not automatically a non-natural use either. The case is a useful corrective to the instinct that any large accumulation of combustible material plus any fire equals liability — Rylands v Fletcher requires the escaping thing to be the thing accumulated, and fire cases sit at the doctrine's edge precisely because it is so often the fire, not the underlying material, that does the travelling.

components.factsShort: A large quantity of tyres stored at a tyre-fitting business accidentally caught fire, which spread to neighbouring property.
components.ratioShort: Rylands v Fletcher requires the thing accumulated by the defendant to escape; where an accidental fire spreads from material that itself never leaves the land, the tyres have not escaped — the fire has, and that is not enough without more.

expanded.facts: A large stock of tyres was stored on the defendant's premises for his tyre-fitting business. A fire started accidentally and spread through the tyres before spreading further to neighbouring premises, causing damage.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that the tyres, the thing said to have been accumulated, never themselves escaped — they burned where they were stored. It was the fire that spread, and fire is not treated as the 'thing' brought onto and kept on land unless the defendant accumulated something inherently and dangerously likely to ignite and spread in that way; ordinary storage of tyres was not such a use, and was not, without more, non-natural either.
expanded.significance: Stannard v Gore is the case to reach for whenever a Rylands v Fletcher fact pattern involves fire. Ask precisely what the defendant accumulated, and whether that thing itself escaped — not just whether fire, once started, travelled off the defendant's land.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often reason that storing a large quantity of any combustible material, plus an accidental fire that spreads, is automatically enough for Rylands v Fletcher.
components.whyItsWrong: The rule requires the thing the defendant accumulated to escape. If the material itself stays put and burns in place, it is the fire — not the material — that crosses onto the neighbour's land, and fire is only treated as the relevant 'thing' where the defendant accumulated something inherently and dangerously prone to ignite and spread, not merely something flammable that happened to catch alight.

interaction.prompt: A garden centre stores a very large quantity of bagged fertiliser, which is chemically unstable and prone to spontaneous combustion at high volumes — a known risk the business is aware of. The fertiliser spontaneously ignites and the resulting fire spreads to a neighbouring property, causing damage. Analyse whether Rylands v Fletcher applies.
factsToOrder: A very large quantity of chemically unstable fertiliser is stored, prone to spontaneous combustion
The business is aware of this specific risk
The fertiliser spontaneously ignites without external cause
Fire spreads to a neighbouring property

scaffolds.support: Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the garden centre is strictly liable under Rylands v Fletcher for fire damage caused by spontaneously combusting fertiliser.
modelAnswer.rule: Rylands v Fletcher requires the defendant to have brought onto and kept on the land something likely to do mischief if it escapes, a non-natural use, an escape of that thing, and reasonably foreseeable damage of that type; where fire is involved, Stannard v Gore requires the thing accumulated itself to be dangerously prone to ignite and spread, not merely combustible material that happened to catch fire.
modelAnswer.application: Unlike the tyres in Stannard v Gore, the fertiliser here is chemically unstable and known by the business to be prone to spontaneous combustion at scale — it is closer to a substance inherently and dangerously likely to ignite and spread than ordinary combustible stock. Storing such a substance in bulk, with knowledge of the specific combustion risk, is capable of being a non-natural use given the scale and known danger. The fire that spreads from the fertiliser can be treated as the escape of the accumulated dangerous thing itself, rather than an unrelated fire merely starting near it. Damage to neighbouring property by fire is a foreseeable type of harm from storing an unstable, combustible substance in bulk.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Unlike Stannard v Gore, this scenario is capable of satisfying Rylands v Fletcher, because the fertiliser itself — not just an incidental fire — is the dangerous thing accumulated, and its ignition and spread is the foreseeable mischief the rule addresses.

testPool.prompt: State the four elements of the rule in Rylands v Fletcher as it stands today.
acceptableAnswers: accumulation of a dangerous thing, non-natural use, escape, foreseeable damage
brings something likely to do mischief, non-natural use, escape, foreseeable type of damage
testPool.modelAnswer: The defendant brings onto and keeps on their land something likely to do mischief if it escapes; the use of the land is non-natural; the thing escapes to land outside the defendant's control; and the damage caused is of a reasonably foreseeable type.

testPool.prompt: Which case added a requirement that the type of damage caused by an escape be reasonably foreseeable?
options: Cambridge Water v Eastern Counties Leather

testPool.prompt: According to Transco v Stockport MBC, how should the tort in Rylands v Fletcher best be characterised?
options: As a freestanding strict liability tort independent of nuisance
As a sub-species of nuisance, applying nuisance-like principles to isolated escapes
As a form of trespass to land
testPool.trapExplanation: It is tempting to keep treating Rylands v Fletcher as its own distinct category of strict liability, since that is how it is often first taught. Transco deliberately rejects that framing, describing the rule as an extension of nuisance to isolated escapes rather than a separate tort.

testPool.prompt: In Rylands v Fletcher itself, what physically escaped from the defendant's land?
In the passage below, adapted from Transco v Stockport MBC, highlight the sentence that states the test for non-natural use.
testPool.passage: The claimant argued that any accumulation likely to cause harm if it escaped should suffice. That submission was rejected. Ordinary domestic water supply, however serious the consequences of its failure, could not be treated as a non-natural use of land. A non-natural use requires something extraordinary or unusual, judged by reference to the time and place, that creates an increased risk to others.
testPool.ratioSentence: A non-natural use requires something extraordinary or unusual, judged by reference to the time and place, that creates an increased risk to others.

testPool.prompt: Order the doctrinal developments from earliest to most recent.
items: Rylands v Fletcher establishes strict liability for escapes from a non-natural use
Cambridge Water requires the type of damage to be reasonably foreseeable
Transco narrows non-natural use and recasts the tort as a sub-species of nuisance
Stannard v Gore clarifies that the thing accumulated, not merely fire, must escape

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that Rylands v Fletcher, as currently understood, imposes liability regardless of whether the type of damage caused was foreseeable?
sliderLabels: Foreseeability of the type of damage is required
testPool.correctPosition: Foreseeability of the type of damage is required
testPool.explanation: Cambridge Water inserted a foreseeability requirement for the type of damage. The tort remains strict as to fault in causing the escape, but not as to whether that kind of harm could have been anticipated.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more closely mirrors the reasoning in Stannard v Gore?
testPool.scenarioA: A business stores a large quantity of ordinary cardboard boxes that accidentally catch fire and burn in place, with the fire then spreading to a neighbouring building.
testPool.scenarioB: A business stores a large tank of highly volatile industrial solvent that itself leaks and flows across the boundary onto neighbouring land.
testPool.explanation: A mirrors Stannard v Gore: the accumulated material (cardboard) stays in place and burns; it is the fire, not the material, that crosses onto the neighbour's land. B is a more conventional Rylands v Fletcher scenario, since the accumulated substance itself physically escapes.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that would most likely prevent this claim succeeding under Rylands v Fletcher.
testPool.scenarioText: A homeowner keeps an ordinary domestic swimming pool in the garden. During an unusually heavy storm, the pool overflows and floods a neighbour's basement.
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right — an ordinary domestic swimming pool is squarely the kind of everyday use Transco treats as natural, much like domestic water supply. Without a non-natural use, the claim cannot get off the ground regardless of the flooding that followed.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on the use of the land, not the flood itself. An ordinary domestic swimming pool is the kind of everyday use Transco treats as natural — the claim is likely to fail at the non-natural use element.

testPool.prompt: A specialist company stores an unusually large quantity of industrial explosives on a site in an otherwise ordinary residential area, for use in nearby quarrying. The explosives detonate accidentally, damaging neighbouring homes. Is the storage likely to be treated as a non-natural use?
options: Yes — storing explosives at scale in a residential-adjacent area is precisely the kind of extraordinary, high-risk use Transco has in mind
No — any lawful commercial activity is automatically treated as natural
It depends solely on whether the company had a licence to store explosives
testPool.explanation: Non-natural use after Transco requires something extraordinary or unusual for the time and place, creating an increased risk to others. Bulk explosives storage in a residential-adjacent area is a clear example, in sharp contrast to the ordinary domestic water supply in Transco itself.

testPool.prompt: A landowner keeps an ornamental garden pond, filled entirely within their own boundary, which never overflows or leaks. A neighbour argues the pond is inherently dangerous and could theoretically flood their property one day. On these facts, can the neighbour succeed in a Rylands v Fletcher claim now?
options: No — there has been no escape at all, which is a distinct, necessary element regardless of how the pond might be characterised
Yes — the mere possibility of a future escape is sufficient
Yes, but only if the pond is later shown to be a non-natural use
testPool.explanation: Without an actual escape, the claim cannot succeed regardless of how the non-natural use question might eventually be resolved — a merely theoretical future risk is not itself damage flowing from an escape that has occurred.

testPool.prompt: A brewery installs a large industrial fermentation tank holding a significant volume of pressurised liquid, well beyond what any ordinary household would keep, in a converted warehouse in a mixed residential-commercial street. A weld fails and the tank's contents burst through a wall into an adjoining flat, causing significant water damage. Analyse the flat owner's position under Rylands v Fletcher.
factsToOrder: A large industrial fermentation tank holds pressurised liquid, well beyond domestic scale
The warehouse is in a mixed residential-commercial street
A weld failure causes the tank's contents to burst through a wall
The contents cause significant water damage to the adjoining flat

Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the flat owner can establish liability under Rylands v Fletcher for damage caused when the fermentation tank's contents burst into the adjoining flat.
modelAnswer.rule: Rylands v Fletcher requires an accumulation of something likely to cause mischief if it escapes, a non-natural use judged by reference to the time and place and the increased risk created, an escape of that thing to land outside the defendant's control, and reasonably foreseeable damage of that type.
modelAnswer.application: The tank holds a significant volume of pressurised liquid well beyond domestic scale, unlike the ordinary water supply in Transco — this points towards non-natural use, particularly given the residential-commercial mix of the street, where such an installation is not the ordinary use of the buildings around it. The weld failure causes the liquid itself, the accumulated thing, to burst through the wall — a clear escape, unlike Stannard v Gore where the accumulated material never itself crossed the boundary. Water damage to an adjoining flat from a bursting pressurised tank is a foreseeable type of harm.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The flat owner has a strong claim under Rylands v Fletcher: the scale and nature of the tank point to non-natural use, the liquid itself escaped, and the resulting water damage was a foreseeable type of harm.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'Rylands v Fletcher imposes liability whenever a defendant keeps something dangerous on their land and it later causes harm off that land.' What is the clearest problem with this statement?
options: It omits the non-natural use and foreseeable-damage-type requirements, both of which narrow the tort considerably
It is entirely correct as a statement of the modern law
It wrongly suggests the defendant must have been at fault in causing the escape
testPool.trapExplanation: This kind of loose summary is common and dangerous in exams — it silently drops both the non-natural use requirement (narrowed sharply by Transco) and the foreseeability of damage type requirement (added by Cambridge Water), leaving something closer to the discredited, overly broad 1868 formulation than the current law.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring error in this lesson's test items is treating Rylands v Fletcher as a simple strict-liability checklist frozen in 1868. Every element after 'escape' has been narrowed by later authority — non-natural use is now genuinely rare, foreseeability of damage type is required, and fire cases need the escaping thing to be the thing accumulated, not just flame that happened to spread.
